short: Sixty years of civil war between Wei, Shu and Wu, and the best-known story in Chinese literature.
full:
The Han dynasty had been a shell for a generation when Cao Pi deposed its last emperor in 220 and declared himself ruler of Wei in the north. Liu Bei, claiming Han descent, answered the next year from Chengdu with the state of Shu Han in the west; Sun Quan took the imperial title in the southeast as Wu in 229. None of the three could finish the others. The decisive engagement had already been fought in 208 at Red Cliffs on the Yangtze, where fireships broke Cao Cao's fleet and fixed the division of China for decades.

The wars were ruinous. Registered households fell by a catastrophic margin, though much of that reflects people slipping off the tax rolls rather than dying. Wei annexed Shu in 263, and in 266 the Sima family took the Wei throne for themselves as the Jin, who conquered Wu in 280 and briefly reunified the country. A fourteenth-century novel, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, made Zhuge Liang, Guan Yu and Cao Cao permanent figures of East Asian culture.
